content: MBD1, or Methyl-CpG-binding domain protein 1, is a protein encoded by the MBD1 gene in humans. This protein specifically binds to methylated sequences in DNA, thereby influencing transcriptional regulation. It has the ability to bind to a variety of methylated DNA sequences and is implicated in the repression of gene expression. MBD1 plays a role in chromatin modification by interacting with the histone H3K9 methyltransferase SETDB1. The modification H3K9me3, which is catalyzed by SETDB1, is known to be a repressive epigenetic mark that contributes to transcriptional silencing. DNA methylation is a critical epigenetic modification in eukaryotic genomes and is essential for mammalian development. The human proteins MECP2, MBD1, MBD2, MBD3, and MBD4 form a family of nuclear proteins characterized by the presence of a methyl-CpG-binding domain (MBD). With the exception of MBD3, all of these proteins can specifically bind to methylated DNA. Among them, MECP2, MBD1, and MBD2 are capable of repressing transcription from methylated gene promoters. The MBD1 gene produces five transcript variants through alternative splicing, resulting in protein isoforms that share a single MBD domain, two to three cysteine-rich (CXXC) domains, and some differences in their C-terminal regions. All five transcript variants are capable of repressing transcription from methylated promoters. Additionally, variants containing three CXXC domains can also repress transcription from unmethylated promoters. MBD1 and MBD2 are located in close proximity to each other on chromosome 18q21. MBD1 has been shown to interact with several proteins, including ATF7IP, CBX5, CHAF1A, and SUV39H1, which may further contribute to its role in chromatin remodeling and transcriptional regulation.
